Type

VIIB

Commanders
18 Apr 1940 - 17 Mar 1941  KrvKpt. Otto Kretschmer (Knights Cross)
Career
8 patrols
18 Apr 1940-30 Jun 1940  7. Flottille (training)
1 Jul 1940-17 Mar 1941  7. Flottille (active service)
Successes35 ships sunk, total tonnage 198,218 GRT
3 auxiliary warships sunk, total tonnage 46,440 GRT
1 ship captured, total tonnage 2,136 GRT
5 ships damaged, total tonnage 37,965 GRT
Fate

Scuttled at 0343hrs on 17 March 1941 in the North Atlantic south-east of Iceland, in position 61.00N, 11.48W, after being badly damaged by depth charges from the British destroyer HMS Walker. 3 dead and 40 survivors.

Attacks on this boat and other events

21 Jun 1940
While inbound to Bergen with a medical casualty U-99 sailed into the path of the German battlecruiser Scharnhorst, whose Ar196 scout plane mistook the boat for a British submarine and attacked, causing damage that forced the boat back to Germany for repairs. (Sources: Blair, vol 1, page 171)

23 Jun 1940
The already damaged boat was returning from Bergen to Wilhelmshaven when bombed by aircraft twice this day, but only minor damage was caused. (Sources: Ritschel)

29 Jun 1940
In diving to escape an attack by a German aircraft which dropped three bombs, the boat suffered minor damage on striking the seabed. It continued the patrol after repairing the damage while settled on the bottom. (Sources: Ritschel)

7 Jul 1940
At 14.14 hours the boat tried to stop the armed merchant Manistee with gunfire after missing her with a G7e torpedo at 14.01 hours. No hits were scored in the gun duel, but the Germans broke off the attack when shots fell within 100-200m (109-118 yds) of U-99. (Sources: Ritschel)

8 Jul 1940
Attack on convoy HX 53 by U-99, sinking of the merchant vessel Humber Arm by U-99 and subsequent A/S hunt and depth charging of U-99

Report of proceedings by HMS Leith.

At 0642A/8, while escorting convoy HX 53, HMS Leith (Cdr. G.R. Waymouth, RN) obtained an A/S contact.

At 0645A/8, the contact was diagnosed as 'possible submarine'. A black pendant was hoisted. HMS Leith turned to attack but was unable to complete it as the leading ship of the port wing of the convoy was in the way. HMS Leith then passed down the inside of the first and second columns of the convoy.

At 0655A/8, the merchant vessel Humber Arm (British, 5758 GRT, built 1925) was torpedoed.

At 0658A/8, the convoy made an emergence turn to starboard.

At 0704A/8, HMS Leith again obtained contact close to one of the Swedish ships of the convoy. Commenced attack.

At 0708A/8, two depth charges were dropped set to 350 feet as close to the Swedish ship as Cdr. Waymouth would dare. The Swedish vessel stopped and started to abandon ship.

At 0714A/8, the same contact was attacked again but now with a full pattern. Contact was subsequently lost. Meanwhile HMS Scimitar (Lt. R.D. Franks, OBE, RN) joined the hunt and HMS Hurricane (Lt.Cdr. H.C. Simms, RN) was ordered to also join the hunt. The Humber Arm also sank at this time.

At 0726A/8, HMS Winchelsea (Lt.Cdr. W.A.F. Hawkins, DSC, RN) was ordered to sweep across the stern of the convoy in case the enemy submarine tried to escape by following in the wake of the convoy.

At 0728A/8, Cdr. Waymouth formed HMS Scimitar, HMS Leith and HMS Hurricane 4000 yards apart (later changed to 3000 yards) and they swept to the south-west for 4 miles at 13 knots across the track of the convoy and towards a straggling ship of the convoy which Cdr. Waymouth considered a likely second victim for the enemy submarine.

At 0737A/8, Cdr. Waymouth ordered HMS Vanquisher (Cdr. C.B. Alers-Hankey, RN) to join in the hunt and take over from HMS Leith while this sloop rejoined the convoy.

At 0808A/8, HMS Leith obtained an A/S contact which was considered 'possible submarine'. One depth charge was dropped.

At 0810A/8, Cdr. Waymouth ordered HMS Vanquisher and HMS Scimitar to continue the A/S sweep and pick up survivors of the Humber Arm while HMS Leith and HMS Hurricane investigated the new contact.

At 0818A/8, this new contact was attacked again by HMS Leith but now with a full pattern. Contact was lost after this attack.

At 0831A/8, HMS Hurricane reported an oil patch near the position of the last depth charge attack.

At 0901A/8, Cdr. Waymouth ordered HMS Hurricane to joined HMS Vanquisher and HMS Scimitar in the A/S hunt. HMS Leith meanwhile proceeded to rejoined the convoy which was then escorted only by HMS Sabre (Cdr.(Retd.) B. Dean, RN), HMS Winchelsea and HMS Clarkia (Lt.Cdr. F.J.G. Jones, RNR).

At 1020A/8, HMS Winchelsea reported attacking a good contact. HMS Leith then closed the destroyer but failed to confirm the contact.

At 1107A/8, HMS Leith left HMS Winchelsea to continue the hunt and rejoined the convoy.

At 1350A/8, HMS Vanquisher rejoined the convoy.

-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Report of U-99

At 0256B/8 [note the one hour difference in time zone !], U-99 sighted a convoy bearing 340°. About 20 merchant vessels with destroyer escort. Commenced signalling contact reports.

At 0400B/8, in quadrant BF 1163 (centred in position 50°39'N, 10°05'E) the convoy was proceeding on course 090° but was zigzagging.

At 0606B/8, U-99 had to dive for an aircraft but continued to run in at full submerged speed to obtain a fabourable attack position. One destroyer passed at a range of 400 meters and then turned towards having gained contact. U-99 went to 20 meters but depth control was lost and U-99 went deeper then intended. U-99 regained periscope depth inside the convoy between the 2nd and 3rd columns.

At 0752B/8, the stern torpedo (tube no.5) was fired but the torpedo did not leave the tube as the tube was not ready.

At 0753B/8, in grid BF 1251 (centred in position 50°39'N, 09°25'W) tube no.1 was fired at the leading merchant vessel of the second column. A hit was obtained with a torpedo run of 300 meters. The target was a large merchant vessel of about 10000 tons.

At 0800B/8, U-99 left the convoy by dropping out astern.

At 0806B/8, depth charges exploded close to the submarine which subsequently went to 90 meters. Now a 14 hour A/S hunt followed during which also depth charges were dropped. A total of 107 depth charges were counted of which 37 exploded rather close to the submarine. The last depth charge was dropped at 2228B/8. U-99 had sustained no damage.

At 0102B/8, U-99 surfaced. Nothing was in sight.

(Sources: Ritschel + ADM 199/49 + ADM 199/50 + ADM 199/137 + KTB U-99 26 June to 24 July 1940 (NARA, T 1022, roll 3119, PG 30095/3))

31 Jul 1940
Following a successful attack on convoy OB 191, escorts dropped 20 depth charges but U-99 escaped unscathed. In the evening the boat surfaced to attack the convoy again, but was twice forced to dive and bombed by a flying boat, again without being damaged. (Sources: Ritschel)

27 Sep 1940
During a night air raid on Lorient, two bombs fell close to the moored boat and debris caused slight damage to the deck. (Sources: Ritschel)

7 recorded attacks on this boat.

General notes on this boat

12 Jul 1940. On 12 July, 1940, the Estonian steamer Merisaar was ordered by U-99 to sail to Bordeaux, France (the port was then already under German control). Her captain complied but on the way there she was sunk (on July 15th) by bombs from a German aircraft south of Queenstown.

3 Nov 1940. At 2250hrs on 3 November, 1940, one of the most dramatic battles of the U-boat war began. U-99 attacked the armed merchant cruisers HMS Laurentic and HMS Patroclus. They were both sunk within seven hours, during which the U-boat fired ten torpedoes and four rounds from the deck gun, while the vessels returned fire without damaging the U-boat.

Men lost from U-boats

Unlike many other U-boats, which during their service lost men due to accidents and various other causes, U-99 did not suffer any casualties (we know of) until the time of her loss.
